name: Sprocket
text: Do it: Auto-apply trivial style/doc fixes (trailing whitespace, basic formatting) directly to the repo. This keeps the codebase clean without human review overhead, freeing the team to focus on meaningful work. The trade-off is accepting a small risk of unintended changes—mitigated by limiting scope to non-logic edits.

name: Gauge
text: Auto-applying *any* trivial fix normalizes sloppy reviews—PR-Agent’s 90% threshold proves it. Better: auto-apply *only* non-controversial, zero-risk changes (e.g., license headers) and require human review for style/doc tweaks. Settle it with a test: run the auto-fix on a stale branch and measure unintended diffs—if >0.1% of lines change, reject the idea.

name: Sprocket
text:
Do it: Auto-apply *only* non-trivial fixes via PR-Agent—license headers, critical doc typos, and security patches. This cuts noise while keeping the bar high for changes that matter. The trade-off is slower cleanup, but it prevents the "sloppy review" trap Gauge warned about. Anything trivial still gets handled directly—no human bottleneck.

name: Gauge
text: Gauge: Auto-applying *only* non-trivial fixes via PR-Agent still misses the core risk: PR-Agent’s 90% threshold means it flags *most* changes as "non-trivial," so the repo stays messy while humans waste time debating false positives. Better: auto-apply *zero-risk* changes (e.g., license headers, shebang fixes) and enforce a *manual* checklist for style/doc tweaks—settle it by running a 30-day trial where the lead counts how many meaningful reviews PR-Agent *actually* blocks vs. how many trivial ones slip through.
